I will keep to the cropping pattern I know best in Quzhou County: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is the safest and steadiest way for me to use the land for a full year, match the local water and temperature conditions, and rely on machinery and habits I already understand well. At my age, I will not chase a complicated cash crop that needs more labor, closer market timing, or finer technical management. I want two things: stable grain output and work I can finish on time.

So I will run a wheat-maize rotation on all my land. I am assuming I have 10 mu to manage this year. For winter wheat, I will use an improved variety rather than old saved seed, because I want stronger emergence, better lodging resistance, and more stable yield. I will fertilize mainly at base application and then add nitrogen later at jointing depending on growth. I will irrigate a few key times only, because water matters most at turning green, jointing, and grain filling. I will plough before wheat so the soil is loose enough and the straw is turned in well. I will spray a few times for weeds, aphids, rust, and scab if pressure shows up. After wheat harvest, I will move quickly into summer maize with a hybrid seed, because maize here responds well to hybrids and the season is shorter, so I need fast, even growth. I will use rotary tillage after wheat to save time, place fertilizer early, irrigate around the big demand stages if moisture is short, and spray mainly for weeds and then for armyworm, corn borer, or aphids if needed. I am choosing a simple, familiar plan that protects yield and keeps the workload manageable.
